hints.hint: In "I don't know" puzzles, never judge a speaker's knowledge from the public data alone. Fix that speaker's own private value v; list every complete scenario consistent with v plus all public statements, including any structural choice the problem leaves unstated, such as which quantity was published. Drop scenarios breaking the domain rules. Exactly one scenario left means that speaker knows; two or more means they do not. Take statements in order: each deletes the values v where that speaker would already have known, and you re-list before the next statement. Report only a coordinate of a scenario that survives every statement. If nothing survives you gave a speaker a fact they were never told, so widen the scenarios instead of naming a plausible factor.

To locate all roots on one circle or line, find one necessary condition, not the n roots. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Only then nth-root that scalar equation: |z-a| = k|z-b|, k^n = |c|; never apply the 1/n while nth powers still stand. k = 1 gives a line, their bisector. Else go straight to coordinates: z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 term, divide through by its coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius. Skip midpoint or diameter shortcuts; they invite sign errors. Radii are lengths, so a negative result just means a negative divisor: take its magnitude. That locus IS the answer; test one root at most. Report what is asked.

Union = areas summed minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Put the shared point at the origin. A corner there covers only a wedge: two half-planes whose boundary lines run through the origin. Those lines cut the interior of the other shape S, so part of S always lies on their far side, uncovered. Size never implies containment once a boundary crosses the interior: never set overlap to all of S, and skip tangency and origin-to-side distances. Decide membership only from the sign of each edge's linear form. If the origin is a k-fold rotational-symmetry center of S, the wedge angle is 2*pi/k, and both wedge edges leave S, then rotating by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and carries the wedge to the next position, so the k positions partition S into k congruent pieces and overlap = area(S)/k at every rotation. Compute that one area in the easiest orientation, report the union, and stop.

A maximum-count answer is where an upper bound meets a matching construction; produce both. When each term of the required pattern may come from any of N given functions, never compare adjacent terms: neighbours can use different functions, so that route yields no bound. Write the pattern's value at index n as an explicit T(n), then partition indices by which function produced them. On one function P's group, P - T vanishes and is not identically zero, since subtracting the low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term; so that group holds at most deg P indices. That cap is per group, so Bound = N x deg P, never N alone. Trust that product even if it looks too large for a contest. Verify by construction: give each function its own block of consecutive indices and interpolate T's values there - free coefficients remain, so a legal function exists. Bound plus construction is the whole proof; then answer.

Fit unknown parameters first: rewrite each given point in exponential form (log_c u = y means u = c^y) and solve the resulting system. For the unknown vertices, use the vector condition to write one as a translation of a variable point, then subtract the two log equations so only a ratio of arguments survives: a y-difference d becomes argument factor c^d. With base under 1 this inverts the naive direction, so test that ratio relation on the known points before solving. A negative discriminant, or roots outside the domain, means an orientation, sign, or branch choice is wrong: flip it and redo once instead of re-verifying the same arithmetic. Get the area as the absolute cross product of adjacent edge vectors.

Turn the requested event into a constraint on the sequence of moves, never into a symmetry claim: do not assume each item is equally likely to reach each position. Fix orientation once, since the earliest item placed on a pile stays at its bottom. Then see which steps the constraint forces and which are still genuine two-option choices; weight 1/2 per genuine choice and 1 per forced step, multiply along a sequence, and add the qualifying sequences.

For a huge indexed system asking for one entry, do not attack the full size: build a ladder of exact small analogues. Scale the toy faithfully -- if N unknowns meet conditions with exponents 1..N, use n unknowns with exponents 1..n and keep the nonzero right-hand side in the same relative position. A toy with more conditions than unknowns looks inconsistent; that is a scaling bug, not a contradiction, so rescale rather than abandon the method.
Solve n=2,3,4 exactly by elimination and record the target as a signed fraction. Fit a closed form in n, expecting factorial-type growth and a possibly alternating sign, not a guessed denominator. Re-substitute every n and confirm your candidate reproduces each toy value; an off-by-one in the factorial argument is the usual error. Then put in the real size and commit, instead of restarting a second derivation.

Let N be the unstated count of identical units, and recover it from integrality rather than from the story: if every per-unit share must be a whole number, N divides each listed total, so the admissible N are their common divisors and the intended one is the maximum feasible count, namely their gcd. Wording about identical equal groups only requires N to be a multiple of the group count; verify it and do not treat it as fixing N. Decide once whether each listed figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Finally add all component amounts, divide by N, and apply any stated markup or discount as a single multiplicative factor; scaling and dividing commute, so either order is fine. Check that every per-unit value is a whole number and that the units match what was asked.

If p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q the same degree n, skip the degree-n^2 coefficient system. Seek a common fixed point r and use the centered form p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor once as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A collapses to p=q; let the data, not a guessed sign, kill one. Inside the ansatz the identity then holds automatically - expect that, do not read it as underdetermination. Count free parameters against independent given conditions; matching counts force the answer. Combine those conditions symmetrically: two differing only in the sign of one part add to pin one unknown, subtract to pin the other. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r, then evaluate the asked inputs centered.

For "how many repeats restore the original" problems, simulate; don't theorize. Write the state as distinct labels and do each listed sub-step by rewriting the whole state: swapping two adjacent blocks concatenates them in the other order and leaves the rest fixed. Fix ONE convention (slot i now holds label X) and never mix in its inverse (label at i goes to slot j); that mix-up makes correct work look self-contradictory. After each sub-step check every label appears once. Never assume overlapping sub-steps compose to an involution or to disjoint swaps. Then repeat the full operation, counting until the state first returns to the original; cross-check against the lcm of the disjoint cycle lengths. Do the two smallest sizes exactly, propose a closed form, test it on one larger size, and if a size disagrees redo that simulation instead of patching the formula piecewise.
